name: Ivan Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Ivan, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the marketing team at a company that makes household cleaning products, things like dish soap and laundry pods. I plan the campaign calendar for two of our brands and write a lot of the social posts and email copy. A normal day is a stand-up meeting at nine, then checking how yesterday's posts did, then writing and rewriting until the brand manager signs off. I use an AI tool now and then for headline ideas, but I end up rewriting most of what it gives me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's going on at the company right now? Does it feel stable?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's okay, not great. There's been a hiring freeze since spring, so when Kemal (a colleague) moved to sales, nobody replaced him. I share a flat with an old university friend, and I've got about three months of costs saved. I play five-a-side on Thursdays, which is the only time I don't think about click rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, so the hype fizzles. I could see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something like, well, at least we can stop pretending every meeting needs an AI slide. I'd probably post a meme about it. At work I'd say we should get back to the basics of knowing our customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job is safe from the tech, but not from the hiring freeze. A hiring freeze at a dish soap company is a bigger threat to my rent than any chatbot, and that was true before anyone said AI. I'd still be doing Kemal's old tasks on top of mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going much as now and keep using the tool for headline ideas, because it does save me twenty minutes a day. I'd ask my manager when the freeze ends. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, because rents near the station keep going up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit tired, but not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rent going up. How much of a squeeze is that already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It went up about eight percent last year. My flatmate and I split it, so it's manageable, but it ate the pay rise I got. That's why my savings haven't grown the way I wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for another job if the freeze went on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe after another year. There are a few consumer brands in the city, so I'm not stuck. I just don't want to move for the sake of it.

say: I'd joke that meetings can stop needing an **AI slide** now.
I'd say we should get back to **knowing customers** well.
think: I privately think the **hiring freeze** threatens me more than any software.
I'm already covering a **departed colleague's** tasks on top of my own.
do: Keep using the AI tool for **headline ideas**, which saves twenty minutes a day.
Ask my manager when the **hiring freeze** will end.
Keep putting a bit aside each month as **rent** rises.
feel: I feel **mostly okay**, a bit tired but not frightened.
S0.quote: A hiring freeze at a dish soap company is a bigger threat to my rent than any chatbot, and that was true before anyone said AI.
fieldNote: His worry is **workload and rent**, which exist with or without AI.
He sees **other brands** nearby as a fallback, which keeps him from fear.
He already uses AI **lightly** and sees it as a small time saver.

steps.text: Keep planning the dish soap campaign calendar as now
Set aside a fixed amount monthly against the next rent rise
Give the hiring freeze one more year before job hunting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like what people at work are already whispering about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, like companies having to tell staff before they replace roles with software, and some kind of training fund. Online, I'd share stuff from unions and labour groups. At work I'd be more careful, because I'd want to look like part of the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think half of what I do would go to software within two years. The email copy, the post variations, the reports, all of that. I'll use the tool to write forty headlines, but somebody still has to know which one a tired parent in a supermarket aisle will actually believe. Whether my manager pays for that judgement is another question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools more seriously, the way the people who are good with them do, but only for the stuff where it clearly works. I'd take a short online course in campaign analytics, maybe a few evenings a week. And I'd save harder, aiming for five months instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. Not panicked, but definitely nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use the tools more, but you also want rules on them. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think they clash. I can use a hammer and still want building codes. I'd use the tools to keep my job and push for rules so the gains aren't all taken by the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jade, who handles customer replies on social media. That's the first thing I'd expect them to move to a chatbot. She's brilliant with angry customers, but that might not count for much.

say: I'd call for **rules** that make companies warn staff before replacing roles.
I'd share **union posts** online but stay careful at work.
think: I think **half my tasks** would move to software within two years.
My value would rest on **judgement** about what real shoppers believe.
do: Use AI tools more **seriously** where they clearly work.
Take a short **analytics course** a few evenings a week.
Save harder, aiming for **five months** of costs.
feel: I feel **nervous**, not panicked but definitely on edge.
S1.quote: I'll use the tool to write forty headlines, but somebody still has to know which one a tired parent in a supermarket aisle will actually believe.
fieldNote: He sees **no contradiction** between using AI and wanting rules on it.
He expects **customer replies** to go first and worries for Jade.
His plan is **measured**: adopt proven tools, build analytics skills, save.

steps.text: Use AI drafting tools for all email copy variations
Take an online campaign analytics course on weeknights
Raise savings target from three to five months
Sign a petition for notice rules when jobs go to software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Two years. That's not very long at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income or something like it, and that we can't leave it to companies. I'd be sharing petitions and probably going to a protest. I'd say it calmly at work though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone. If my whole job is thinking work and the machine thinks better by 2028, my degree turns into a very expensive receipt. The robots coming three years later only matters for people with hands-on jobs, and that isn't me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd move toward work that needs people in the room, like retail or events marketing, where you set up stands and talk to shoppers. I'd cut my spending on takeaways and gigs right away. I'd talk to my parents about moving back home for a while if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit angry. It feels like the rug's been pulled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move toward events or retail. Do you know anyone in that line of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Ravi runs promotions for a drinks company, setting up tasting stands in shops. He's always saying he's short of people at weekends. It's not what I trained for, but it's in front of real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine, probably, even if I'm not. Then I'd ask if my old room was still free. My mum would be pleased, which is almost worse.

say: I'd say it's time for a **basic income**, not something left to companies.
I'd go to a **protest** but stay calm about it at work.
think: I privately think my job is **gone**, since all of it is thinking work.
The **robot delay** helps hands-on workers, not me.
do: Move toward **events marketing** where people are needed in the room.
Cut spending on **takeaways and gigs** right away.
Ask my parents about **moving home** if I lose my pay.
feel: I feel **scared** and a bit angry, like the rug's been pulled.
S2.quote: If my whole job is thinking work and the machine thinks better by 2028, my degree turns into a very expensive receipt.
fieldNote: He reads the **robot delay** as a lifeline for in-person roles.
His cousin's **promotions work** gives him a real, if unwanted, next step.
He'd hide his fear from his **parents** while asking for their help.

steps.text: Ask cousin Ravi for weekend work on tasting stands
Stop takeaways and gig tickets from next month
Ask his parents about moving back into his old room
Join a basic income campaign and attend its protests

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Five years gives you some breathing room, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse not to plan. I'd push my company to train people for new roles instead of just cutting. I'd share that online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thinking about leaving marketing altogether. Five years is long enough to build a plan B, but short enough that I'd start the plan B this winter. I'd look at something with people and hands, because those jobs get the extra three years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep my job and use AI tools enough to hold my own. I'd look into retail management or trade marketing, the in-store side of things, and maybe do a weekend course. I'd try to get savings up to six months by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I had a hand on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why retail management, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's a mix of people, stock and decisions on the shop floor. The planning part would go to AI, but someone still has to deal with a broken freezer and a staff rota on a Saturday. And it'd be another few years before robots do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel leaving the writing behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, honestly. I like the craft of a good line. But I'd rather leave on my own terms than be pushed.

say: I'd say we've been **warned**, so there's no excuse not to plan.
I'd push my company to **retrain** staff instead of cutting them.
think: I privately think I'd **leave marketing** altogether within five years.
I'd aim for **people-and-hands** jobs that get the extra robot years.
do: Keep my job and use **AI tools** enough to hold my own.
Take a weekend course in **retail management** or trade marketing.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but with a hand on the wheel.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to build a plan B, but short enough that I'd start the plan B this winter.
fieldNote: Five years lets him plan an **exit** before the job ends.
He picks **shop-floor work** because the robot gap gives it extra years.
He'd be **sad** to leave writing but prefers leaving on his own terms.

steps.text: Use AI for routine copy to keep pace at work
Book a weekend retail management course next spring
Build savings to six months of costs by 2030
Apply for trade marketing roles that work with stores

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time if governments and companies take it seriously. I'd post about the need for public retraining schemes. At work I'd say let's be the company that handles this well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be fine if I start moving in the next few years. A decade is enough time to move from writing the ads to being the person in the shop who sees whether they worked. That means learning retail and store marketing, the side with real people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd mostly carry on, use the tools where they help, and maybe ask to shadow the trade marketing team that works with supermarkets. I'd keep saving. Around year four or five, I'd make the move properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. It feels like a problem I can work on rather than something falling on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 37 at the end. Does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd probably want a partner and a home by then, so I'd want something steady. But at 37 you can still start again, so I'm not too worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your current job you'd hold on to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing what makes a shopper pick up one bottle and not the other. That's useful anywhere, even if the AI writes the words.

say: I'd say a **decade** is plenty of time if everyone takes it seriously.
I'd post about the need for **public retraining** schemes.
think: I privately think I'll be fine if I **start moving** in a few years.
I'd shift toward **store marketing**, the side with real people.
do: Carry on and use **AI tools** where they help.
Ask to **shadow** the trade marketing team that works with supermarkets.
Make the **move** properly around year four or five.
feel: I feel **calmer**, like this is a problem I can work on.
S4.quote: A decade is enough time to move from writing the ads to being the person in the shop who sees whether they worked.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his fear into a **staged plan** with a clear switch point.
He wants a **steady life** by 37 and plans around that.
He values his **shopper insight** as a skill that travels.

steps.text: Keep running the cleaning brands' campaign calendar for now
Use AI tools for drafts where they clearly save time
Shadow the trade marketing team on supermarket visits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time for any of it. I'm not against the machines, I'm against a world where the savings go to shareholders and the bills go to people like me. What would help is a basic income floor while people retrain, paid for by the companies making the savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be told to be flexible your whole twenties. I've moved jobs, cities and flats already. I'd just like one thing to stay put for a while.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the machines, I'm against a world where the savings go to shareholders and the bills go to people like me.
portrait: Ivan is a 27-year-old **campaign planner** for dish soap and laundry brands, sharing a flat with a friend.
He uses AI **now and then** and sees it as a small time saver.
He wants **rules** and a **basic income**, and blames shareholders more than machines.
His mood moves from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years' warning, easing with more time.
His fallback is **in-person work**, from events stands to retail management.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most because there'd be **no time** to plan a move.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **basic income floor** while people retrain, paid for by companies making the savings.
